2. Fourier and Convolution

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Convolution combines shifted copies of a signal, but evaluating it directly can be costly and obscure the structure of the operation. Fourier coordinates turn convolution into multiplication, providing both efficient algorithms and a way to solve differential equations. We develop this connection on continuous and finite domains, study sampling and the fast Fourier transform, and extend the viewpoint to groups, surfaces, and graphs.

The main reference for this chapter is [23].

2.1 Hilbert Spaces and Fourier Transforms¶

2.1.1 Orthonormal Bases¶

Many methods in data science begin by expanding the input signal in a basis. An orthonormal basis gives a simple reconstruction formula and preserves energy, which simplifies the analysis. We first describe these properties in a Hilbert space, such as H=L2([0,1]d)\mathcal{H}=L^2([0,1]^d)H=L2([0,1]d) for signals on a continuous domain or H=RN\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^NH=RN for discrete signals.

A complex Hilbert space (H,⟨⋅, ⋅⟩)(\mathcal{H},\langle \cdot,\,\cdot\rangle)(H,⟨⋅,⋅⟩) is complete for the norm induced by its Hermitian inner product. We take this inner product to be linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. A separable Hilbert space admits an orthonormal basis (φk)k(\varphi_k)_k(φk​)k​ (finite in finite dimension), so every f∈Hf\in\mathcal{H}f∈H has the expansion

f=∑k⟨f, φk⟩φkf = \sum_{k} \langle f,\,\varphi_k\rangle \varphi_kf=k∑​⟨f,φk​⟩φk​

where the norm is determined by ∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣2:=⟨f, f⟩|\!| f |\!|^2 \mathrel{:=}\langle f,\,f\rangle∣∣f∣∣2:=⟨f,f⟩. Convergence means that ∣ ⁣∣f−∑k=0N⟨f, φk⟩φk∣ ⁣∣→0|\!| f - \sum_{k=0}^N \langle f,\,\varphi_k\rangle \varphi_k |\!| \rightarrow 0∣∣f−∑k=0N​⟨f,φk​⟩φk​∣∣→0 as N→+∞N \rightarrow +\inftyN→+∞. Parseval’s identity expresses conservation of energy:

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣2=∑k∣⟨f, φk⟩∣2.|\!| f |\!|^2 = \sum_k |\langle f,\,\varphi_k\rangle|^2.∣∣f∣∣2=k∑​∣⟨f,φk​⟩∣2.

The Gram–Schmidt procedure constructs such a basis from a linearly independent family (φˉk)k(\bar\varphi_k)_k(φˉ​k​)k​ with dense span. Set φ0=φˉ0/∣ ⁣∣φˉ0∣ ⁣∣\varphi_0=\bar\varphi_0/|\!| \bar\varphi_0 |\!|φ0​=φˉ​0​/∣∣φˉ​0​∣∣ and φk=φ~k/∣ ⁣∣φ~k∣ ⁣∣\varphi_k=\tilde\varphi_k/|\!| \tilde\varphi_k |\!|φk​=φ~​k​/∣∣φ~​k​∣∣, where φ~k\tilde\varphi_kφ~​k​ is the orthogonal residual φ~k=φˉk−∑i<kaiφi\tilde\varphi_k=\bar\varphi_k - \sum_{i<k} a_i \varphi_iφ~​k​=φˉ​k​−∑i<k​ai​φi​. Orthogonality requires ai=⟨φˉk, φi⟩a_i = \langle \bar \varphi_k,\,\varphi_i\rangleai​=⟨φˉ​k​,φi​⟩.

On L2([−1,1])L^2([-1,1])L2([−1,1]) with the usual inner product, orthogonalizing the monomials gives the Legendre polynomials. Their conventional normalization differs from unit L2L^2L2 norm:

φ0(x)=1,φ1(x)=x,φ2(x)=12(3x2−1),etc.\varphi_0(x)=1, \quad \varphi_1(x)=x, \quad \varphi_2(x) = \frac{1}{2}(3x^2-1), \quad \text{etc.}φ0​(x)=1,φ1​(x)=x,φ2​(x)=21​(3x2−1),etc.

On L2(R,e−x2/2 dx)L^2(\mathbb{R},e^{-x^2/2}\,\mathrm{d}x)L2(R,e−x2/2dx), this construction gives the probabilists’ Hermite polynomials P0(x)=1P_0(x)=1P0​(x)=1, P1(x)=xP_1(x)=xP1​(x)=x, P2(x)=x2−1P_2(x)=x^2-1P2​(x)=x2−1, up to normalization. Multiplying normalized polynomials by e−x2/4e^{-x^2/4}e−x2/4 instead gives orthonormal Hermite functions for Lebesgue measure. A degree-kkk orthogonal polynomial has exactly kkk distinct real zeros in the interior of the support of the measure.

The Shannon interpolation theorem gives another example: (sinc(x−k))k( \mathop{\mathrm{sinc}}(x-k) )_k(sinc(x−k))k​ is an orthonormal basis of the subspace {f∈L2(R)  ;  supp(f^)⊂[−π,π]}\left\{ f\in L^2(\mathbb{R}) \;;\; \mathop{\mathrm{supp}}(\hat f) \subset [-\pi,\pi] \right\}{f∈L2(R);supp(f^​)⊂[−π,π]}. Using the continuous representative of fff, the reconstruction formula f=∑kf(k)sinc(x−k)f=\sum_k f(k) \mathop{\mathrm{sinc}}(x-k)f=∑k​f(k)sinc(x−k) identifies the coefficients as ⟨f, sinc(x−k)⟩=f(k)\langle f,\,\mathop{\mathrm{sinc}}(x-k)\rangle = f(k)⟨f,sinc(x−k)⟩=f(k). The series converges in L2L^2L2 and pointwise; the previous chapter proves the pointwise formula under additional decay assumptions.

Orthogonal bases can also arise as complete families of eigenvectors of self-adjoint operators. Below, we explain how translation-invariant operators (convolutions) characterize Fourier bases.

2.1.2 Fourier Basis on R/2πZ\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}R/2πZ¶

Fourier analysis takes different forms on different domains. On the circle, it gives a countable orthonormal basis. On the real line, frequencies form a continuum, and the Fourier transform is not an expansion in a countable basis of exponential functions.

On L2(T)L^2(\mathbb{T})L2(T) where T=R/2πZ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}T=R/2πZ, equipped with ⟨f, g⟩:=12π∫Tf(x)gˉ(x)dx\langle f,\,g\rangle \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\mathbb{T}f(x) \bar g(x) \mathrm{d}x⟨f,g⟩:=2π1​∫T​f(x)gˉ​(x)dx, one can use the Fourier basis

φk(x):=eikxfork∈Z.(2.1)\varphi_k(x) \mathrel{:=}e^{\mathrm{i}k x} \quad \text{for} \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \tag{2.1}φk​(x):=eikxfork∈Z.(2.1)

One thus has

f=∑k∈Zf^keik⋅wheref^k:=12π∫02πf(x)e−ikxdx,(2.2)f = \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} \hat f_k e^{\mathrm{i}k \cdot} \quad \text{where} \quad \hat f_k \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x) e^{-\mathrm{i}k x} \mathrm{d}x, \tag{2.2}f=k∈Z∑​f^​k​eik⋅wheref^​k​:=2π1​∫02π​f(x)e−ikxdx,(2.2)

with convergence in L2(T)L^2(\mathbb{T})L2(T). Pointwise convergence is delicate; see Section 1.2.

∀ ω∈R,f^(ω):=∫Rf(x)e−ixωdx.\forall \,\omega\in \mathbb{R}, \quad \hat f(\omega) \mathrel{:=}\int_\mathbb{R}f(x) e^{-\mathrm{i}x \omega} \mathrm{d}x.∀ω∈R,f^​(ω):=∫R​f(x)e−ixωdx.

f(x)⟶Ff^(ω)sampling↓↓periodization(f(n))n⟶Fourier series∑nf(n)e−iωn.\begin{array}{rcccl} & f(x) & \overset{\mathcal{F}}{\longrightarrow} & \hat f(\omega) &\\ \text{sampling}& \downarrow & & \downarrow &\text{periodization} \\ & (f(n))_n & \overset{\text{Fourier series}}{\longrightarrow} & \sum_n f(n) e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega n} &\\ \end{array}.sampling​f(x)↓(f(n))n​​⟶F​⟶Fourier series​​f^​(ω)↓∑n​f(n)e−iωn​periodization​.

∑nf(n)e−iωn=∑nf^(ω−2πn)(2.3)\sum_n f(n) e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega n} = \sum_n \hat f(\omega-2\pi n) \tag{2.3}n∑​f(n)e−iωn=n∑​f^​(ω−2πn)(2.3)

2.2.1 Convolution¶

Figure 2.3. Convolution on R\mathbb{R}R. The dashed curve is f⋆gf\star gf⋆g; the marked value (f⋆g)(x)(f\star g)(x)(f⋆g)(x) equals the shaded integral.

f⋆g(x)=∫Xf(t)g(x−t)dt.(2.4)f \star g(x) = \int_\mathbb{X}f(t) g(x-t) \mathrm{d}t. \tag{2.4}f⋆g(x)=∫X​f(t)g(x−t)dt.(2.4)

Here and throughout this section, integrals use Lebesgue measure on R\mathbb{R}R and normalized Haar measure dt/(2π)\mathrm{d}t/(2\pi)dt/(2π) on T\mathbb{T}T. With this convention, Young’s inequality states that, for 1⩽p,q,r⩽∞1\leqslant p,q,r\leqslant\infty1⩽p,q,r⩽∞ and (f,g)∈Lp(X)×Lq(X)(f,g)\in L^p(\mathbb{X})\times L^q(\mathbb{X})(f,g)∈Lp(X)×Lq(X),

Proposition 2.1

If f,g∈L1(X)f,g\in L^1(\mathbb{X})f,g∈L1(X), then

F(f⋆g)=f^⊙g^.(2.6)\mathcal{F}(f \star g) = \hat f \odot \hat g. \tag{2.6}F(f⋆g)=f^​⊙g^​.(2.6)

For X=R\mathbb{X}=\mathbb{R}X=R, ⊙\odot⊙ denotes pointwise multiplication of the continuous Fourier transforms. For X=T\mathbb{X}=\mathbb{T}X=T, ⊙\odot⊙ acts on bounded Fourier-coefficient sequences (pointwise multiplication of sequences).

Figure 2.6. How the Fourier transform converts convolution into multiplication.

This means that F\mathcal{F}F is an algebra homomorphism. For instance, if X=R\mathbb{X}=\mathbb{R}X=R, its range lies in the algebra of continuous functions that vanish at ±∞\pm\infty±∞.

As shown in Figure 2.7, successive convolutions of a box function produce cardinal splines: piecewise polynomials of increasing smoothness.

Figure 2.7. Cardinal splines are defined by successive convolutions.

Convolution also describes the sum of independent random variables. Writing fXf_XfX​ for the probability density of a random vector XXX with respect to Lebesgue measure, independence of XXX and YYY gives fX+Y=fX⋆fYf_{X+Y}=f_X \star f_YfX+Y​=fX​⋆fY​. This identity is fundamental in probability and statistics.

2.2.2 Translation Invariant Operators¶

Figure 2.8. Commutative diagram for translation invariance.

Translation-invariant operators commute with translations. In signal and image processing, they apply the same rule at every location.

The following propositions characterize translation-invariant operators as convolutions against kernels that may be distributions. The term “translation equivariant” is more precise: translating the input translates the output by the same amount.

The kernel’s regularity depends on the topologies of the input and output spaces, so the proof differs between the two settings below.

We begin with operators whose outputs are continuous functions.

Conversely, by Parseval’s identity, a bounded sequence ccc defines a bounded Fourier multiplier, which commutes with translations. Translation-invariant operators are therefore diagonal in the Fourier basis.

2.2.3 Poisson’s Formula and Distributions¶

Informally, the Fourier series

∑nf(n)e−iωn\sum_n f(n) e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega n}n∑​f(n)e−iωn

for s>0s>0s>0, where δa\delta_aδa​ is the Dirac mass at location a∈Ra \in \mathbb{R}a∈R, i.e. the distribution such that ∫f dδa=f(a)\int f\,\mathrm{d}\delta_a=f(a)∫fdδa​=f(a) for any continuous fff. A measure can be multiplied by a continuous function; a general distribution can be multiplied by a smooth function. For a tempered distribution μ\muμ, its Fourier transform is defined by duality on Schwartz test functions:

∀ g∈S(R),∫Rg(x)dF(μ)=∫RF(g)dμ,whereF(g):=∫Rg(x)e−ix⋅ dx,\forall \,g \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}), \quad \int_\mathbb{R}g(x) \mathrm{d}\mathcal{F}(\mu) = \int_\mathbb{R}\mathcal{F}(g) \mathrm{d}\mu, \quad \text{where} \quad \mathcal{F}(g) \mathrel{:=}\int_\mathbb{R}g(x)e^{-\mathrm{i}x\cdot}\,\mathrm{d}x,∀g∈S(R),∫R​g(x)dF(μ)=∫R​F(g)dμ,whereF(g):=∫R​g(x)e−ix⋅dx,

Here S(R)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})S(R) is the Schwartz space; the integral notation denotes the distributional pairing.

The Poisson formula (2.3) can thus be interpreted as

F(Π1⊙f)=∑nf^(⋅−2πn)=∫Rf^(⋅−ω)dΠ2π(ω)=f^⋆Π2π\mathcal{F}(\Pi_1 \odot f) = \sum_n \hat f(\cdot-2\pi n) = \int_\mathbb{R}\hat f(\cdot-\omega) \mathrm{d}\Pi_{2\pi}(\omega) = \hat f \star \Pi_{2\pi}F(Π1​⊙f)=n∑​f^​(⋅−2πn)=∫R​f^​(⋅−ω)dΠ2π​(ω)=f^​⋆Π2π​

2.3 Finite Fourier Transform and Convolution¶

2.3.1 Discrete Orthonormal Bases¶

A discrete signal is a finite-dimensional vector f∈CNf \in \mathbb{C}^Nf∈CN, where NNN is the number of samples and fnf_nfn​ is the value at a specified location. For a 2-D image f∈CN≃CN0×N0f \in \mathbb{C}^N \simeq \mathbb{C}^{N_0 \times N_0}f∈CN≃CN0​×N0​, we have N=N0×N0N = N_0 \times N_0N=N0​×N0​, with N0N_0N0​ pixels in each direction.

The discrete inner product is the analogue of the continuous L2L^2L2 inner product:

⟨f, g⟩=∑n=0N−1fngˉn.\langle f,\,g\rangle = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n \bar g_n.⟨f,g⟩=n=0∑N−1​fn​gˉ​n​.

The corresponding squared Euclidean distance is

∣ ⁣∣f−g∣ ⁣∣2=∑n=0N−1∣fn−gn∣2.|\!| f-g |\!|^2 = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |f_n-g_n|^2.∣∣f−g∣∣2=n=0∑N−1​∣fn​−gn​∣2.

Exactly as in the continuous case, a discrete orthonormal basis {ψk}0⩽k<N\{ \psi_k \}_{0 \leqslant k < N }{ψk​}0⩽k<N​ of CN\mathbb{C}^NCN satisfies

⟨ψk, ψk′⟩=δk−k′.(2.7)\langle \psi_k,\,\psi_{k'}\rangle = \delta_{k-k'}. \tag{2.7}⟨ψk​,ψk′​⟩=δk−k′​.(2.7)

A signal expands in this orthonormal basis as

f=∑k=0N−1⟨f, ψk⟩ψk.f = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \langle f,\,\psi_k\rangle \psi_k.f=k=0∑N−1​⟨f,ψk​⟩ψk​.

It preserves energy

∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣2=∑n=0N−1∣fn∣2=∑k=0N−1∣⟨f, ψk⟩∣2|\!| f |\!|^2 = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |f_n|^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} |\langle f,\,\psi_k\rangle|^2∣∣f∣∣2=n=0∑N−1​∣fn​∣2=k=0∑N−1​∣⟨f,ψk​⟩∣2

Computing the set of all inner products {⟨f, ψk⟩}0⩽k<N\{\langle f,\,\psi_k\rangle\}_{0 \leqslant k < N}{⟨f,ψk​⟩}0⩽k<N​ directly requires O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) operations. This cost is prohibitive when NNN reaches millions of samples. Structured bases permit faster decompositions: Fourier and wavelet transforms require O(Nlog⁡(N))O(N\log(N))O(Nlog(N)) and O(N)O(N)O(N) operations, respectively.

We denote f=(fn)n=0N−1∈RNf = (f_n)_{n=0}^{N-1} \in \mathbb{R}^Nf=(fn​)n=0N−1​∈RN, and regard its entries as indexed by n∈Z/NZn \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}n∈Z/NZ, which is a finite abelian group under addition. This corresponds to using periodic boundary conditions.

∀ k=0,…,N−1,f^k:=∑n=0N−1fne−2iπNkn=⟨f, φk⟩whereφk:=(e2iπNkn)n=0N−1∈CN(2.8)\forall \,k=0,\ldots,N-1, \quad \hat f_k \mathrel{:=}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n e^{-\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}kn} = \langle f,\,\varphi_k\rangle \quad \text{where} \quad \varphi_k \mathrel{:=}( e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}kn} )_{n=0}^{N-1} \in \mathbb{C}^N \tag{2.8}∀k=0,…,N−1,f^​k​:=n=0∑N−1​fn​e−N2iπ​kn=⟨f,φk​⟩whereφk​:=(eN2iπ​kn)n=0N−1​∈CN(2.8)

where the canonical inner product on CN\mathbb{C}^NCN is ⟨u, v⟩=∑n=0N−1unvˉn\langle u,\,v\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}u_n\bar v_n⟨u,v⟩=∑n=0N−1​un​vˉn​ for (u,v)∈(CN)2(u,v) \in (\mathbb{C}^N)^2(u,v)∈(CN)2.

This definition is motivated by sampling the Fourier basis x↦eikxx \mapsto e^{\mathrm{i}k x}x↦eikx on R/2πZ\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}R/2πZ at equally spaced points (2πNn)n=0N−1( \frac{2\pi}{N}n )_{n=0}^{N-1}(N2π​n)n=0N−1​.

One has

⟨φk, φℓ⟩={Nifk=ℓ,0otherwise.\langle \varphi_k,\,\varphi_\ell\rangle = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} N \quad \text{if} \quad k=\ell, \\ 0 \quad\text{otherwise.} \end{array} \right.⟨φk​,φℓ​⟩={Nifk=ℓ,0otherwise.​

∀ n=0,…,N−1,fn=1N∑kf^ke2iπNkn.(2.9)\forall \,n=0,\ldots,N-1, \quad f_n = \frac{1}{N}\sum_k \hat f_k e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}kn}. \tag{2.9}∀n=0,…,N−1,fn​=N1​k∑​f^​k​eN2iπ​kn.(2.9)

which is the sum of a geometric series (equivalently, the sum of equispaced points on a circle).

Assuming N=2N′N=2N'N=2N′, one has

f^2k=∑n=0N′−1(fn+fn+N/2)e−2iπN′knf^2k+1=∑n=0N′−1e−2iπNn(fn−fn+N/2)e−2iπN′kn.\begin{aligned} \hat f_{2k} &= \sum_{n=0}^{N'-1} (f_n + f_{n+N/2}) e^{ -\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N'} k n } \\ \hat f_{2k+1} &= \sum_{n=0}^{N'-1} e^{ -\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N} n } (f_n - f_{n+N/2}) e^{ -\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N'} k n }. \end{aligned}f^​2k​f^​2k+1​​=n=0∑N′−1​(fn​+fn+N/2​)e−N′2iπ​kn=n=0∑N′−1​e−N2iπ​n(fn​−fn+N/2​)e−N′2iπ​kn.​

Introduce the vectors fe=(fn+fn+N/2)n∈CN′f_e = (f_n + f_{n+N/2})_n \in \mathbb{C}^{N'}fe​=(fn​+fn+N/2​)n​∈CN′ and fo=(fn−fn+N/2)n∈CN′f_o = (f_n - f_{n+N/2})_n \in \mathbb{C}^{N'}fo​=(fn​−fn+N/2​)n​∈CN′ and the twiddle factors αN=(e−2iπn/N)n=0N′−1∈CN′\alpha_N=(e^{-2\mathrm{i}\pi n/N})_{n=0}^{N'-1}\in\mathbb{C}^{N'}αN​=(e−2iπn/N)n=0N′−1​∈CN′. The recursion becomes

FN(f)=IN(FN/2(fe),FN/2(fo⊙αN))\mathcal{F}_N(f) = \mathcal{I}_N( \mathcal{F}_{N/2}(f_e), \mathcal{F}_{N/2}(f_o \odot \alpha_N) )FN​(f)=IN​(FN/2​(fe​),FN/2​(fo​⊙αN​))

where IN\mathcal{I}_NIN​ is the “interleaving” operator, defined by IN(a,b):=(a0,b0,a1,b1,…,aN′−1,bN′−1)\mathcal{I}_N(a,b) \mathrel{:=}(a_0,b_0,a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_{N'-1},b_{N'-1})IN​(a,b):=(a0​,b0​,a1​,b1​,…,aN′−1​,bN′−1​).

Recursing yields the radix-two fast Fourier transform (FFT) when NNN is a power of two. Other FFT factorizations handle general lengths. Zero-padding to a power of two is also useful, although it changes the transform length and the sampled frequencies.

This algorithm can also be interpreted as a factorization of the Fourier matrix into a product of O(log⁡N)O(\log N)O(logN) sparse matrices.

2ℓT(ℓ)=2×2ℓ−1T(ℓ−1)+2ℓK⟹T(ℓ)=T(ℓ−1)+K⟹T(ℓ)=T(0)+Kℓ2^\ell T(\ell) = 2 \times 2^{\ell-1} T(\ell-1) + 2^\ell K \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T(\ell) = T(\ell-1) + K \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T(\ell) = T(0) + K \ell2ℓT(ℓ)=2×2ℓ−1T(ℓ−1)+2ℓK⟹T(ℓ)=T(ℓ−1)+K⟹T(ℓ)=T(0)+Kℓ

2.3.4 Finite convolution¶

For (f,g)∈(RN)2(f,g) \in (\mathbb{R}^{N})^2(f,g)∈(RN)2, one defines f⋆g∈RNf\star g \in \mathbb{R}^Nf⋆g∈RN as

∀ n=0,…,N−1,(f⋆g)n:=∑k=0N−1fkgn−k=∑k+ℓ=nfkgℓ(2.11)\forall \,n=0,\ldots,N-1, \quad (f \star g)_n \mathrel{:=}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} f_k g_{n-k} = \sum_{k+\ell=n} f_k g_\ell \tag{2.11}∀n=0,…,N−1,(f⋆g)n​:=k=0∑N−1​fk​gn−k​=k+ℓ=n∑​fk​gℓ​(2.11)

where +++ and −-− are interpreted modulo NNN (vectors are defined on the group Z/NZ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}Z/NZ, or equivalently, one uses periodic boundary conditions).

This defines a commutative algebra structure (RN,+,⋆)(\mathbb{R}^N,+,\star)(RN,+,⋆), with neutral element the “Dirac” δ0:=(1,0,…,0)⊤∈RN\delta_0 \mathrel{:=}(1,0,\ldots,0)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^Nδ0​:=(1,0,…,0)⊤∈RN. The following proposition shows that F:f↦f^\mathcal{F}: f \mapsto \hat fF:f↦f^​ is an algebra isomorphism and an isometry (up to a scaling by N\sqrt{N}N​ of the norm) from (CN,+,⋆)(\mathbb{C}^N,+,\star)(CN,+,⋆) onto (CN,+,⊙)(\mathbb{C}^N,+,\odot)(CN,+,⊙) with neutral element 1N=(1,…,1)∈RN\mathbb{1}_N=(1,\ldots,1) \in \mathbb{R}^N1N​=(1,…,1)∈RN.

Proposition 2.5

One has F(f⋆g)=f^⊙g^\mathcal{F}( f \star g ) = \hat f \odot \hat gF(f⋆g)=f^​⊙g^​.

Proof

We denote T:g↦f⋆gT : g \mapsto f \star gT:g↦f⋆g. One has

(Tφℓ)n=(f⋆φℓ)n=∑pfpe2iπNℓ(n−p)=e2iπNℓnf^ℓ=f^ℓ(φℓ)n.(T \varphi_\ell)_n = (f \star \varphi_\ell)_n = \sum_p f_p e^{ \frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}\ell(n-p) } = e^{ \frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}\ell n } \hat f_\ell = \hat f_\ell (\varphi_\ell)_n.(Tφℓ​)n​=(f⋆φℓ​)n​=p∑​fp​eN2iπ​ℓ(n−p)=eN2iπ​ℓnf^​ℓ​=f^​ℓ​(φℓ​)n​.

Thus (φℓ)ℓ(\varphi_\ell)_\ell(φℓ​)ℓ​ form a basis of NNN eigenvectors of TTT, with eigenvalues f^ℓ\hat f_\ellf^​ℓ​. The operator TTT is diagonal in this basis. Let F=(e−2iπNkn)k,nF=( e^{ -\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}k n } )_{k,n}F=(e−N2iπ​kn)k,n​ be the Fourier transform matrix. The inversion formula (2.9) gives F−1=1NF∗F^{-1} = \frac{1}{N}F^*F−1=N1​F∗, where F∗=Fˉ⊤F^*=\bar F^\topF∗=Fˉ⊤ is the adjoint (conjugate transpose). The diagonalization of TTT is therefore

T=F−1diag(f^)F⟹F(Tg)=diag(f^)Fg⟹F(f⋆g)=diag(f^)g^.T = F^{-1} \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\hat f) F \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal{F}(T g) = \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\hat f) F g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal{F}(f \star g) = \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\hat f) \hat g.T=F−1diag(f^​)F⟹F(Tg)=diag(f^​)Fg⟹F(f⋆g)=diag(f^​)g^​.

This proposition gives an O(Nlog⁡N)O(N\log N)O(NlogN) convolution algorithm:

f⋆g=F−1(f^⊙g^).f \star g = \mathcal{F}^{-1}( \hat f \odot \hat g ).f⋆g=F−1(f^​⊙g^​).

When ∣Supp(g)∣=P|\mathop{\mathrm{Supp}}(g)|=P∣Supp(g)∣=P is small, direct evaluation costs O(PN)O(PN)O(PN) and may be faster. An example is g=[1,1,0,…,0,1]/3g=[1,1,0,\ldots,0,1]/3g=[1,1,0,…,0,1]/3, the moving average, where

(f⋆g)n=fn−1+fn+fn+13(f \star g)_n = \frac{f_{n-1}+f_n+f_{n+1}}{3}(f⋆g)n​=3fn−1​+fn​+fn+1​​

needs 3N3N3N operations.

Convolution as translation invariant operator.

Define translation on Z/NZ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}Z/NZ by (Tτf)n:=fn−τ(T_\tau f)_n \mathrel{:=}f_{n-\tau}(Tτ​f)n​:=fn−τ​, with n−τn-\taun−τ computed modulo NNN. The next proposition is the finite counterpart of the results on R\mathbb{R}R and R/2πZ\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}R/2πZ. On Z/NZ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}Z/NZ, no convergence issues arise, and the impulse response can be defined directly.

Proposition 2.6

Let H:RN→RNH:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^NH:RN→RN be linear. Then H∘Tτ=Tτ∘HH \circ T_\tau = T_\tau \circ HH∘Tτ​=Tτ​∘H for all τ\tauτ if and only if there exists h∈RNh \in \mathbb{R}^Nh∈RN (often called the impulse response) so that Hf=f⋆hHf = f \star hHf=f⋆h.

Proof

For the convolution-to-invariance implication, we first note that Tτf=f⋆δτT_\tau f=f\star\delta_\tauTτ​f=f⋆δτ​ is a convolution against a translated Dirac δτ=Tτ(δ)\delta_\tau=T_\tau(\delta)δτ​=Tτ​(δ) where δ=(1,0,…,0)\delta=(1,0,\ldots,0)δ=(1,0,…,0). If Hf=f⋆hHf=f\star hHf=f⋆h, commutativity gives

H∘Tτ(f)=h⋆δτ⋆f=δτ⋆h⋆f=Tτ∘H(f).H \circ T_\tau(f) = h \star \delta_\tau \star f = \delta_\tau \star h \star f = T_\tau \circ H(f).H∘Tτ​(f)=h⋆δτ​⋆f=δτ​⋆h⋆f=Tτ​∘H(f).

Conversely, we define h:=H(δ)h \mathrel{:=}H(\delta)h:=H(δ). Then

Polynomial multiplication.

The FFT can multiply large polynomials. It can also multiply large integers by interpreting their digit expansions in a fixed base as polynomials. Indeed,

(∑i=0AaiXi)(∑j=0BbjXj)=∑k=0A+B(∑i+j=kaibj)Xk(\sum_{i=0}^A a_i X^i)(\sum_{j=0}^B b_j X^j) = \sum_{k=0}^{A+B} ( \sum_{i+j=k} a_i b_j ) X^k(i=0∑A​ai​Xi)(j=0∑B​bj​Xj)=k=0∑A+B​(i+j=k∑​ai​bj​)Xk

Setting aside the carry operation, which can be performed in linear time, one can write ∑i+j=kaibj=(aˉ⋆bˉ)k\sum_{i+j=k} a_i b_j = (\bar a \star \bar b)_k∑i+j=k​ai​bj​=(aˉ⋆bˉ)k​ when one defines aˉ,bˉ∈RA+B+1\bar a,\bar b\in\mathbb{R}^{A+B+1}aˉ,bˉ∈RA+B+1 by zero padding.

2.4 Discretization Issues¶

The FFT also approximates the continuous Fourier transform and its inverse. Reversing the roles of space and frequency leads to an efficient spectral interpolation method.

2.4.1 Fourier approximation via spatial zero padding.¶

The discrete Fourier transform (2.8) approximates samples of the continuous Fourier transform (1.2). For a sufficiently smooth fff supported on [0,1][0,1][0,1], consider the vector fQ:=(f(n/N))n=0Q−1∈RQf^Q \mathrel{:=}(f(n/N))_{n=0}^{Q-1} \in \mathbb{R}^QfQ:=(f(n/N))n=0Q−1​∈RQ. Taking Q⩾NQ\geqslant NQ⩾N pads the original samples with zeros, since continuity and the support condition give f(n/N)=0f(n/N)=0f(n/N)=0 for n⩾Nn\geqslant Nn⩾N. For signed frequency indices −⌊Q/2⌋⩽k⩽⌈Q/2⌉−1-\lfloor Q/2\rfloor\leqslant k\leqslant\lceil Q/2\rceil-1−⌊Q/2⌋⩽k⩽⌈Q/2⌉−1 and T=Q/NT=Q/NT=Q/N,

1Nf^kQ=1N∑n=0N−1f(n/N)e−2πink/Q≈∫01f(x)e−2πikx/T dx=f^(2πk/T).\begin{aligned} \frac1N\hat f_k^Q &=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(n/N)e^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}nk/Q}\\ &\approx\int_0^1f(x)e^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}kx/T}\,\mathrm{d}x =\hat f(2\pi k/T). \end{aligned}N1​f^​kQ​​=N1​n=0∑N−1​f(n/N)e−2πink/Q≈∫01​f(x)e−2πikx/Tdx=f^​(2πk/T).​

For a fixed physical frequency, the Riemann-sum error is O(1/N)O(1/N)O(1/N) for f∈C1f\in C^1f∈C1. The bound need not be uniform over frequencies growing with NNN. Increasing QQQ at fixed NNN samples the same spectrum more densely; it does not increase the Nyquist frequency.

2.4.2 Fourier interpolation via spectral zero padding.¶

One can reverse the roles of space and frequency in the previous construction.

Given NNN uniform discrete samples fN=(fnN)n=0N−1f^N=(f^N_n)_{n=0}^{N-1}fN=(fnN​)n=0N−1​, one can compute their discrete Fourier transform F(fN)=f^N\mathcal{F}(f^N) = \hat f^NF(fN)=f^​N (in O(Nlog⁡(N))O(N \log(N))O(Nlog(N)) operations with the FFT),

f^kN:=∑n=0N−1fnNe−2iπNnk,\hat f^N_k \mathrel{:=}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f^N_n e^{-\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N} n k},f^​kN​:=n=0∑N−1​fnN​e−N2iπ​nk,

and then zero-pad the spectrum to obtain a vector of length Q⩾NQ\geqslant NQ⩾N.

For simplicity, assume that N=2N′+1N=2N'+1N=2N′+1 is odd. Even lengths admit a similar, slightly more involved construction.

With frequency indices −N′⩽k⩽N′-N'\leqslant k\leqslant N'−N′⩽k⩽N′, define the padded spectrum by

f~kQ=f^kN(−N′⩽k⩽N′),f~kQ=0otherwise,f~Q∈CQ\tilde f_k^Q=\hat f_k^N\quad(-N'\leqslant k\leqslant N'),\qquad\tilde f_k^Q=0\quad\text{otherwise},\qquad\tilde f^Q\in\mathbb{C}^Qf~​kQ​=f^​kN​(−N′⩽k⩽N′),f~​kQ​=0otherwise,f~​Q∈CQ

The signed frequency indices are interpreted modulo QQQ when calling an FFT routine. An inverse transform of size QQQ, multiplied by Q/NQ/NQ/N, then gives in O(Qlog⁡Q)O(Q\log Q)O(QlogQ) operations

2.5 Fourier in Multiple Dimensions¶

Tensor products extend the one-dimensional Fourier transform to any finite dimension d>1d>1d>1.

2.5.1 On Continuous Domains¶

On Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd.

Figure 2.13. 2-D sine wave.

Tensor products retain a useful feature of Fourier atoms: a product of elementary 1-D complex exponentials is a plane wave

∏ℓ=1deixℓωℓ=ei⟨x, ω⟩\prod_{\ell=1}^d e^{ \mathrm{i}x_\ell \omega_\ell } = e^{ \mathrm{i}\langle x,\,\omega\rangle }ℓ=1∏d​eixℓ​ωℓ​=ei⟨x,ω⟩

whose constant-phase hyperplanes are orthogonal to the wave vector ω=(ωℓ)ℓ=1d∈Rd\omega=(\omega_\ell)_{\ell=1}^d \in \mathbb{R}^dω=(ωℓ​)ℓ=1d​∈Rd when this vector is nonzero. Here ⟨x, ω⟩=∑ℓxℓωℓ\langle x,\,\omega\rangle = \sum_\ell x_\ell \omega_\ell⟨x,ω⟩=∑ℓ​xℓ​ωℓ​ is the canonical inner product on Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd.

The Fourier transform and its inverse are defined by

∀ ω∈Rd,f^(ω):=∫Rdf(x)e−i⟨x, ω⟩dx,∀ x∈Rd,f(x)=1(2π)d∫Rdf^(ω)ei⟨x, ω⟩ dω,\begin{aligned} \forall \,\omega\in \mathbb{R}^d, \quad \hat f(\omega) &\mathrel{:=}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x) e^{-\mathrm{i}\langle x,\,\omega\rangle} \mathrm{d}x, \\ \forall \,x \in \mathbb{R}^d, \quad f(x) &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^d} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\hat f(\omega)e^{\mathrm{i}\langle x,\,\omega\rangle}\,\mathrm{d}\omega, \end{aligned}∀ω∈Rd,f^​(ω)∀x∈Rd,f(x)​:=∫Rd​f(x)e−i⟨x,ω⟩dx,=(2π)d1​∫Rd​f^​(ω)ei⟨x,ω⟩dω,​

under the same integrability assumptions as in one dimension.

Figure 2.14. 2D Fourier orthogonal bases.

On (R/2πZ)d(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^d(R/2πZ)d.

Given an orthonormal basis (φn1)n1∈N(\varphi_{n_1})_{n_1 \in \mathbb{N}}(φn1​​)n1​∈N​ of L2(X)L^2(\mathbb{X})L2(X), one constructs an orthonormal basis of L2(Xd)L^2(\mathbb{X}^d)L2(Xd) by tensorization

∀ k=(k1,…,kd)∈Nd,∀ x∈Xd,φk(x)=φk1(x1)…φkd(xd).(2.12)\forall \,k=(k_1,\ldots,k_d) \in \mathbb{N}^d, \quad \forall \,x \in \mathbb{X}^d, \quad \varphi_k(x) = \varphi_{k_1}(x_1) \ldots \varphi_{k_d}(x_d). \tag{2.12}∀k=(k1​,…,kd​)∈Nd,∀x∈Xd,φk​(x)=φk1​​(x1​)…φkd​​(xd​).(2.12)

Fubini’s theorem gives orthogonality. Completeness gives convergence of the rectangular partial sums ∑∣ ⁣∣k∣ ⁣∣∞⩽N⟨f, φk⟩φk→f\sum_{|\!| k |\!|_\infty \leqslant N} \langle f,\,\varphi_k\rangle \varphi_k \rightarrow f∑∣∣k∣∣∞​⩽N​⟨f,φk​⟩φk​→f in L2(Xd)L^2(\mathbb{X}^d)L2(Xd).

For the multidimensional torus (R/2πZ)d(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^d(R/2πZ)d, using the Fourier basis (2.1), this gives the basis

We describe the algorithm for d=2d=2d=2; the same construction works in any finite dimension.

A fast algorithm for orthogonal decompositions in two 1-D bases (φk11)k1=1N1(\varphi_{k_1}^{1})_{k_1=1}^{N_1}(φk1​1​)k1​=1N1​​, (φk22)k2=1N2(\varphi_{k_2}^{2})_{k_2=1}^{N_2}(φk2​2​)k2​=1N2​​ also gives a fast decomposition in the tensor product basis (φk11⊗φk22)k1,k2(\varphi_{k_1}^{1} \otimes \varphi_{k_2}^{2})_{k_1,k_2}(φk1​1​⊗φk2​2​)k1​,k2​​: apply the algorithm first to the rows and then to the columns of the matrix (fn)n=(n1,n2)∈RN1×N2(f_n)_{n=(n_1,n_2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_1 \times N_2}(fn​)n=(n1​,n2​)​∈RN1​×N2​. If C(N1)C(N_1)C(N1​) is the cost of the 1-D algorithm on RN1\mathbb{R}^{N_1}RN1​, the resulting 2-D transform costs N2C(N1)+N1C(N2)N_2 C(N_1)+N_1 C(N_2)N2​C(N1​)+N1​C(N2​). f^=FN1×f×FN2⊤∈CN1×N2.\hat f = F_{N_1} \times f \times F_{N_2}^{\top}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_1\times N_2}.f^​=FN1​​×f×FN2​⊤​∈CN1​×N2​.

2.5.3 Shannon sampling theorem.¶

Theorem 1.2 extends to sampling on a uniform Cartesian grid in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd by tensorization. Use the continuous representative of the bandlimited function fff. In two dimensions, if supp(f^)⊂[−π/s1,π/s1]×[−π/s2,π/s2]\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}(\hat f) \subset [-\pi/s_1,\pi/s_1] \times [-\pi/s_2,\pi/s_2]supp(f^​)⊂[−π/s1​,π/s1​]×[−π/s2​,π/s2​] and fff decays sufficiently fast,

∀ x∈R2,f(x)=∑n∈Z2f(n1s1,n2s2)sinc(x1/s1−n1)sinc(x2/s2−n2)wheresinc(u)=sin⁡(πu)πu.\forall \,x \in \mathbb{R}^2, \quad f(x) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^2} f(n_1 s_1,n_2 s_2) \mathop{\mathrm{sinc}}(x_1/s_1-n_1) \mathop{\mathrm{sinc}}(x_2/s_2-n_2) \quad \text{where} \quad \mathop{\mathrm{sinc}}(u) = \frac{\sin(\pi u)}{\pi u}.∀x∈R2,f(x)=n∈Z2∑​f(n1​s1​,n2​s2​)sinc(x1​/s1​−n1​)sinc(x2​/s2​−n2​)wheresinc(u)=πusin(πu)​.

2.5.4 Convolution in higher dimension.¶

Convolution on Xd\mathbb{X}^dXd, for X=R\mathbb{X}=\mathbb{R}X=R or X=R/2πZ\mathbb{X}=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}X=R/2πZ, is defined as in one dimension:

f⋆g(x)=∫Xdf(t)g(x−t)dt.f \star g(x) = \int_{\mathbb{X}^d} f(t) g(x-t) \mathrm{d}t.f⋆g(x)=∫Xd​f(t)g(x−t)dt.

Similarly, finite discrete convolution of vectors f∈RN1×N2f \in \mathbb{R}^{N_1 \times N_2}f∈RN1​×N2​ extends formula (2.11) as

2.7 A Bit of Group Theory¶

The reference for this section is [26].

2.7.1 Characters¶

For (G,+)(G,+)(G,+) a commutative group, a character is a group morphism χ:(G,+)→(C∗,⋅)\chi : (G,+) \rightarrow (\mathbb{C}^*,\cdot)χ:(G,+)→(C∗,⋅), i.e. it satisfies

∀ (n,m)∈G,χ(n+m)=χ(n)χ(m).\forall \,(n,m) \in G, \quad \chi(n+m) = \chi(n)\chi(m).∀(n,m)∈G,χ(n+m)=χ(n)χ(m).

The characters form the dual group (G^,⊙)(\hat G,\odot)(G^,⊙) under pointwise multiplication (χ1⊙χ2)(n):=χ1(n)χ2(n)(\chi_1 \odot \chi_2)(n) \mathrel{:=}\chi_1(n) \chi_2(n)(χ1​⊙χ2​)(n):=χ1​(n)χ2​(n). The inverse of a character χ\chiχ is χ−1(n)=χ(−n)\chi^{-1}(n)=\chi(-n)χ−1(n)=χ(−n).

For a finite group GGG with ∣G∣=N|G|=N∣G∣=N, we have N×n=0N \times n=0N×n=0 for every n∈Gn \in Gn∈G. Consequently, χ(n)N=χ(Nn)=χ(0)=1\chi(n)^N=\chi(N n)=\chi(0)=1χ(n)N=χ(Nn)=χ(0)=1: characters take values among the roots of unity,

χ(n)∈{e2iπNk  ;  0⩽k⩽N−1}.(2.19)\chi(n) \in \left\{ e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}k} \;;\; 0 \leqslant k \leqslant N-1 \right\} . \tag{2.19}χ(n)∈{eN2iπ​k;0⩽k⩽N−1}.(2.19)

Thus G^\hat GG^ is a finite group (since there are finitely many maps between two finite sets) and χ−1=χˉ\chi^{-1}=\bar\chiχ−1=χˉ​. In the case of a cyclic group, the dual is simple to describe.

Proposition 2.7

For G=Z/NZG=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}G=Z/NZ, the dual is G^=(φk)k=0N−1\hat G=( \varphi_k )_{k=0}^{N-1}G^=(φk​)k=0N−1​, where φk=(e2iπNnk)n\varphi_k=( e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}nk} )_nφk​=(eN2iπ​nk)n​. The map k↦φkk \mapsto \varphi_kk↦φk​ defines a noncanonical isomorphism G∼G^G \sim \hat GG∼G^.

Proof

The φk\varphi_kφk​ are indeed characters.

Conversely, for any χ∈G^\chi \in \hat Gχ∈G^, according to (2.19), χ(1)=e2iπNk\chi(1)=e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}k}χ(1)=eN2iπ​k for some kkk. Then

χ(n)=χ(1)n=e2iπNkn=φk(n).\chi(n)=\chi(1)^n=e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}k n} = \varphi_k(n).χ(n)=χ(1)n=eN2iπ​kn=φk​(n).

These characters are distinct because the values φk(1)\varphi_k(1)φk​(1) are distinct. Hence ∣G∣=∣G^∣|G|=|\hat G|∣G∣=∣G^∣, and the displayed map is an isomorphism.

This proposition thus shows that characters of cyclic groups are exactly the orthogonal discrete Fourier basis defined in (2.8).

Commutative groups.

The structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups expresses every such group as a product of cyclic groups:

G∼(Z/N1Z)×…×(Z/NdZ)×ZQ.(2.20)G \sim (\mathbb{Z}/N_1\mathbb{Z}) \times \ldots \times (\mathbb{Z}/N_d\mathbb{Z}) \times \mathbb{Z}^Q. \tag{2.20}G∼(Z/N1​Z)×…×(Z/Nd​Z)×ZQ.(2.20)

If GGG is finite, then Q=0Q=0Q=0 and N=N1⋯NdN=N_1\cdots N_dN=N1​⋯Nd​. In this case, GGG is simply a discrete ddd-dimensional “rectangle” with periodic boundary conditions.

For two finite groups (G1,G2)(G_1,G_2)(G1​,G2​) one has

G1×G2^=G^1⊗G^2={χ1⊗χ2  ;  (χ1,χ2)∈G^1×G^2}.(2.21)\widehat{G_1 \times G_2} = \hat G_1 \otimes \hat G_2 = \left\{ \chi_1 \otimes \chi_2 \;;\; (\chi_1,\chi_2) \in \hat G_1 \times \hat G_2 \right\} . \tag{2.21}G1​×G2​​=G^1​⊗G^2​={χ1​⊗χ2​;(χ1​,χ2​)∈G^1​×G^2​}.(2.21)

Here ⊗\otimes⊗ is the tensor product of two functions

∀ (n1,n2)∈G1×G2,(χ1⊗χ2)(n1,n2):=χ1(n1)χ2(n2).\forall \,(n_1,n_2) \in G_1 \times G_2, \quad (\chi_1 \otimes \chi_2)(n_1,n_2) \mathrel{:=}\chi_1(n_1)\chi_2(n_2).∀(n1​,n2​)∈G1​×G2​,(χ1​⊗χ2​)(n1​,n2​):=χ1​(n1​)χ2​(n2​).

The tensor product χ1⊗χ2\chi_1 \otimes \chi_2χ1​⊗χ2​ is a character. Conversely, every character has the factorization χ=χ(⋅,0)⊗χ(0,⋅)\chi=\chi(\cdot,0) \otimes \chi(0,\cdot)χ=χ(⋅,0)⊗χ(0,⋅), since (n1,n2)=(n1,0)+(0,n2)(n_1,n_2)=(n_1,0)+(0,n_2)(n1​,n2​)=(n1​,0)+(0,n2​).

Combining this factorization with the structure theorem proves the following isomorphism.

Proposition 2.8

If GGG is commutative and finite then G^∼G\hat G \sim GG^∼G.

Proof

The structure theorem (2.20) with Q=0Q=0Q=0 and the product-duality identity (2.21) give

G^∼G^1⊗…⊗G^d\hat G \sim \hat G_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes \hat G_dG^∼G^1​⊗…⊗G^d​

where Gℓ:=Z/NℓZG_\ell \mathrel{:=}\mathbb{Z}/N_\ell\mathbb{Z}Gℓ​:=Z/Nℓ​Z.

One then observes that G^1⊗G^2∼G^1×G^2\hat G_1 \otimes \hat G_2 \sim \hat G_1 \times \hat G_2G^1​⊗G^2​∼G^1​×G^2​.

Proposition 2.7 then completes the proof, since G^k∼Gk\hat G_k \sim G_kG^k​∼Gk​.

The isomorphism G^∼G\hat G \sim GG^∼G is noncanonical: it depends on a choice of generators and corresponding roots of unity. As in vector-space duality, the double-dual isomorphism G^^∼G\hat{\hat{G}} \sim GG^^∼G is canonical and is given by evaluation:

g∈G⟼eg∈G^^where(eg:χ∈G^↦χ(g)∈C∗.)g \in G \longmapsto e_g \in \hat{\hat{G}} \quad \text{where} \quad \left( e_g : \chi \in \hat G \mapsto \chi(g) \in \mathbb{C}^*. \right)g∈G⟼eg​∈G^^where(eg​:χ∈G^↦χ(g)∈C∗.)

Discrete Fourier transform from the Character Viewpoint.

This construction also identifies the Fourier basis explicitly. The characters in G^ℓ\hat G_\ellG^ℓ​ are the discrete Fourier atoms (2.8), of the form

(e2iπNℓkℓnℓ)nℓ=0Nℓ−1for some0⩽kℓ<Nℓ.( e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N_\ell} k_\ell n_\ell})_{n_\ell=0}^{N_\ell-1} \quad\text{for some}\quad 0 \leqslant k_\ell < N_\ell.(eNℓ​2iπ​kℓ​nℓ​)nℓ​=0Nℓ​−1​for some0⩽kℓ​<Nℓ​.

Identifying GGG and G1×…×GdG_1 \times \ldots \times G_dG1​×…×Gd​, their tensor products show that the characters in G^\hat GG^ form exactly the orthogonal multidimensional Fourier basis (2.13).

2.7.2 More General cases¶

Infinite groups.

For an infinite finitely generated abelian group, the structure theorem has Q>0Q>0Q>0. For locally compact abelian groups, the dual consists of continuous characters with values on the unit circle; invariant Haar measure determines integration. For G=ZG=\mathbb{Z}G=Z, the characters have a continuous frequency parameter,

Z^={φω:n↦einω∈CZ  ;  ω∈R/2πZ}\hat{\mathbb{Z}}= \left\{ \varphi_\omega: n \mapsto e^{\mathrm{i}n \omega} \in \mathbb{C}^\mathbb{Z} \;;\; \omega\in \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} \right\}Z^={φω​:n↦einω∈CZ;ω∈R/2πZ}

so that Z^∼R/2πZ\hat{\mathbb{Z}}\sim \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}Z^∼R/2πZ.

The case G=ZQG=\mathbb{Z}^QG=ZQ follows by tensorization.

The (φω)ω(\varphi_\omega)_\omega(φω​)ω​ are “orthogonal” in the sense that ⟨φω, φω′⟩Z=2πδ2π(ω−ω′)\langle \varphi_\omega,\,\varphi_{\omega'}\rangle_\mathbb{Z}=2\pi\delta_{2\pi}(\omega-\omega')⟨φω​,φω′​⟩Z​=2πδ2π​(ω−ω′) can be understood as a Dirac kernel (this is similar to the Poisson formula), where ⟨u, v⟩Z:=∑nunvˉn\langle u,\,v\rangle_\mathbb{Z}\mathrel{:=}\sum_n u_n \bar v_n⟨u,v⟩Z​:=∑n​un​vˉn​.

Expanding a sequence (cn)n∈Z(c_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}(cn​)n∈Z​ in characters amounts to forming the Fourier series ∑ncne−inω\sum_n c_n e^{-\mathrm{i}n \omega}∑n​cn​e−inω.

Similarly, for G=R/2πZG=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}G=R/2πZ, one has G^=Z\hat G=\mathbb{Z}G^=Z, with orthonormal characters φn=ei⋅n\varphi_n=e^{\mathrm{i}\cdot n}φn​=ei⋅n, so that the decomposition of functions in L2(G)L^2(G)L2(G) is the computation of Fourier coefficients.

On a compact group, normalized invariant measure provides the natural L2L^2L2 inner product.

Non-commutative groups.

For a noncommutative group, one-dimensional characters do not recover GGG. For example, the symmetric group ΣN\Sigma_NΣN​ on N⩾2N\geqslant 2N⩾2 letters has only the characters G^={1,ε}\hat G=\{1,\varepsilon\}G^={1,ε}, where ε(σ)=(−1)q\varepsilon(\sigma) = (-1)^{q}ε(σ)=(−1)q is the signature and qqq is the number of transpositions in a decomposition of σ∈ΣN\sigma\in \Sigma_Nσ∈ΣN​.

To study noncommutative groups, replace homomorphisms χ:G→C∗\chi : G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^*χ:G→C∗ by homomorphisms ρ:G→GL(Cnρ)\rho : G \rightarrow \text{GL}(\mathbb{C}^{n_\rho})ρ:G→GL(Cnρ​) for some nρn_\rhonρ​. These are called representations of GGG. For (g,g′)∈G(g,g') \in G(g,g′)∈G, writing the group operation multiplicatively on GGG, the defining identity is ρ(gg′)=ρ(g)∘ρ(g′)\rho(gg')=\rho(g) \circ \rho(g')ρ(gg′)=ρ(g)∘ρ(g′). When nρ=1n_\rho=1nρ​=1, the identification GL(C)∼C∗\text{GL}(\mathbb{C}) \sim \mathbb{C}^*GL(C)∼C∗ recovers the one-dimensional characters. For any representation ρ\rhoρ, the function χ(g):=tr(ρ(g))\chi(g) \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho(g))χ(g):=tr(ρ(g)), where tr\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}tr denotes trace, is called its character. This trace function is generally not a group homomorphism.

For a finite group GGG, every subspace VVV invariant under all ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) admits an invariant complement WWW, so that Cnρ=V⊕W\mathbb{C}^{n_\rho}=V\oplus WCnρ​=V⊕W with WWW also invariant. In a basis adapted to these subspaces, the representation matrices are block diagonal. To construct the complement, use the inner product

⟨x, y⟩:=∑g∈G⟨ρ(g)x, ρ(g)y⟩Cnρ\langle x,\,y\rangle \mathrel{:=}\sum_{g \in G} \langle \rho(g)x,\,\rho(g)y\rangle_{\mathbb{C}^{n_\rho}}⟨x,y⟩:=g∈G∑​⟨ρ(g)x,ρ(g)y⟩Cnρ​​

and take the orthogonal complement V⊥V^\botV⊥ for this inner product. In an orthonormal basis of Cnρ\mathbb{C}^{n_\rho}Cnρ​ for this product, all matrices ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) are unitary.

A representation is irreducible if it has no nonzero proper invariant subspace. These are the elementary representations from which larger ones are built by block-diagonal assembly.

We identify irreducible representations up to isomorphism: (ρ,ρ′)(\rho,\rho')(ρ,ρ′) are isomorphic if ρ′(g)=U−1ρ(g)U\rho'(g)=U^{-1}\rho(g)Uρ′(g)=U−1ρ(g)U for every ggg, with a single change-of-basis matrix U∈GL(Cd)U \in \text{GL}(\mathbb{C}^d)U∈GL(Cd). Their isomorphism classes form the unitary dual, denoted G^\hat GG^, which is generally a set rather than a group.

For the symmetric group, there is an explicit description of the set of irreducible representations.

For example, G=Σ3G=\Sigma_3G=Σ3​ has ∣G∣=6|G|=6∣G∣=6 elements. It has two one-dimensional representations, the trivial representation and the signature, and one two-dimensional irreducible representation obtained by identifying GGG with the isometries of an equilateral triangle in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2. Their dimensions satisfy 6=∣G∣=∑nρ2=1+1+226 = |G| = \sum n_\rho^2 = 1+1+2^26=∣G∣=∑nρ2​=1+1+22.

The dimensions nρn_\rhonρ​ of the irreducible representations ρ∈G^\rho\in\hat Gρ∈G^ satisfy ∑ρ∈G^nρ2=N\sum_{\rho \in \hat G} n_\rho^2 = N∑ρ∈G^​nρ2​=N. After choosing unitary representatives, their matrix entries form an orthogonal basis for functions f:G→Cf : G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}f:G→C. This basis is noncanonical because it depends on a choice of basis within each representation.

The associated Fourier transform of a function f:G→Cf:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C}f:G→C is defined as

∀ ρ∈G^,f^(ρ):=∑g∈Gf(g)ρ(g)∈Cnρ×nρ.\forall \,\rho \in \hat G, \quad \hat f(\rho) \mathrel{:=}\sum_{g \in G} f(g) \rho(g) \in \mathbb{C}^{n_\rho \times n_\rho}.∀ρ∈G^,f^​(ρ):=g∈G∑​f(g)ρ(g)∈Cnρ​×nρ​.

With this sign convention, these are pairings with conjugated matrix entries. Their orthogonality makes the transform invertible.

The next proposition gives the inverse transform.

Proposition 2.9

One has

∀ g∈G,f(g)=1∣G∣∑ρ∈G^nρtr(f^(ρ)ρ(g−1)).\forall \,g \in G, \quad f(g) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\rho \in \hat G} n_\rho \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}( \hat f(\rho) \rho(g^{-1}) ).∀g∈G,f(g)=∣G∣1​ρ∈G^∑​nρ​tr(f^​(ρ)ρ(g−1)).
Proof

The proof uses the regular-character identity, valid for every g∈Gg\in Gg∈G

Ag:=∑ρ∈G^nρtr(ρ(g))=∣G∣δgA_g \mathrel{:=}\sum_{\rho \in \hat G} n_\rho \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho(g))=|G|\delta_gAg​:=ρ∈G^∑​nρ​tr(ρ(g))=∣G∣δg​

where δg=0\delta_g=0δg​=0 for g≠IdGg \neq \mathrm{Id}_Gg=IdG​ and δIdG=1\delta_{\mathrm{Id}_G}=1δIdG​​=1. A proof is given in the book by Diaconis, p. 13: decompose the character of the regular representation into irreducible characters and use their orthogonality. The regular representation acts by permuting, according to GGG, the canonical basis of R∣G∣\mathbb{R}^{|G|}R∣G∣.

One then has

1∣G∣∑ρ∈G^nρtr(f^(ρ)ρ(g−1))=1∣G∣∑ρ∈G^nρtr(∑uf(u)ρ(u)ρ(g−1))=∑uf(u)1∣G∣∑ρ∈G^nρtr(ρ(ug−1))=∑uf(u)Aug−1/∣G∣=f(g).\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\rho \in \hat G} n_\rho \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}( \hat f(\rho) \rho(g^{-1}) ) &= \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\rho \in \hat G} n_\rho \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}( \sum_u f(u) \rho(u) \rho(g^{-1}) ) \\ &= \sum_u f(u) \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{\rho \in \hat G} n_\rho \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}( \rho(u g^{-1}) ) = \sum_u f(u)A_{ug^{-1}}/|G| = f(g). \end{aligned}∣G∣1​ρ∈G^∑​nρ​tr(f^​(ρ)ρ(g−1))​=∣G∣1​ρ∈G^∑​nρ​tr(u∑​f(u)ρ(u)ρ(g−1))=u∑​f(u)∣G∣1​ρ∈G^∑​nρ​tr(ρ(ug−1))=u∑​f(u)Aug−1​/∣G∣=f(g).​

One can define the convolution of two functions f,h:G→Cf,h : G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}f,h:G→C as

(f⋆h)(a):=∑bc=af(b)h(c)(f \star h)(a) \mathrel{:=}\sum_{bc=a} f(b) h(c)(f⋆h)(a):=bc=a∑​f(b)h(c)

Convolution need not be commutative on this group. The Fourier transform block-diagonalizes the convolution operators, as stated next.

Proposition 2.10

Denoting F(f)=f^\mathcal{F}(f) = \hat fF(f)=f^​

F(f⋆h)(ρ)=f^(ρ)×h^(ρ)\mathcal{F}(f \star h)(\rho) = \hat f(\rho) \times \hat h(\rho)F(f⋆h)(ρ)=f^​(ρ)×h^(ρ)

where ×\times× denotes matrix multiplication.

where we made the change of variable z=y−1xz=y^{-1}xz=y−1x.

Fast algorithms for computing f^\hat ff^​ exist for some groups, including permutation groups. Their structure is considerably more involved than for G=Z/NZG=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}G=Z/NZ.

For infinite compact groups, the theory uses a discrete infinite family of irreducible representations. The rotation group SO(3)(3)(3) is a useful example. Its representations can be described explicitly through the spherical harmonics introduced in Section 2.8.2. There is one representation of dimension 2ℓ+12\ell+12ℓ+1 for each frequency index ℓ\ellℓ.

2.8 A Bit of Spectral Theory¶

On a general domain X\mathbb{X}X, the group-theoretic approach applies when X=G\mathbb{X}=GX=G is a group or when a group acts transitively on X\mathbb{X}X. Another approach defines Fourier-like basis functions as eigenfunctions of a differential operator, following the characterization in Section 2.6. The Laplacian is particularly useful: it is second order, rotation invariant, and has natural counterparts on surfaces and graphs.

2.8.1 On a Surface or a Manifold¶

Figure 2.20. Computing the Laplacian on a surface.

Let X\mathbb{X}X be a smooth compact connected Riemannian manifold of dimension ddd, without boundary. The Laplace–Beltrami operator can be characterized, for smooth fff, by the small-ball mean-value expansion

(Δf)(x)=lim⁡ε→02(d+2)ε2(1Vol(Bε(x))∫Bε(x)f(y) dμ(y)−f(x)).(\Delta f)(x)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\frac{2(d+2)}{\varepsilon^2} \left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{Vol}(B_\varepsilon(x))}\int_{B_\varepsilon(x)}f(y)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(y)-f(x)\right).(Δf)(x)=ε→0lim​ε22(d+2)​(Vol(Bε​(x))1​∫Bε​(x)​f(y)dμ(y)−f(x)).

0=λ0>λ1⩾λ2⩾⋯⟶−∞.0=\lambda_0>\lambda_1\geqslant\lambda_2\geqslant\cdots\longrightarrow-\infty.0=λ0​>λ1​⩾λ2​⩾⋯⟶−∞.

2.8.2 Spherical Harmonics¶

Figure 2.21. Spherical coordinates.

Consider the (d−1)(d-1)(d−1)-dimensional sphere Sd−1={x∈Rd  ;  ∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣Rd=1}\mathbb{S}^{d-1} = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^d \;;\; |\!| x |\!|_{\mathbb{R}^d}=1 \right\}Sd−1={x∈Rd;∣∣x∣∣Rd​=1}.

The Laplacian has explicit eigenfunctions. For d=3d=3d=3, they are indexed by n=(ℓ,m)n=(\ell,m)n=(ℓ,m):

∀ ℓ∈N,∀ m=−ℓ,…,ℓ,φℓ,m(θ,φ)=eimφPℓm(cos⁡(θ))\forall \,\ell \in \mathbb{N}, \quad \forall \,m=-\ell,\ldots,\ell, \quad \varphi_{\ell,m}(\theta,\varphi) = e^{\mathrm{i}m \varphi} P_{\ell}^m( \cos(\theta) )∀ℓ∈N,∀m=−ℓ,…,ℓ,φℓ,m​(θ,φ)=eimφPℓm​(cos(θ))

The corresponding eigenvalue is λℓ,m=−ℓ(ℓ+1)\lambda_{\ell,m} = -\ell(\ell+1)λℓ,m​=−ℓ(ℓ+1). Here PℓmP_{\ell}^mPℓm​ are associated Legendre functions (polynomials multiplied by (1−x2)∣m∣/2(1-x^2)^{|m|/2}(1−x2)∣m∣/2). Normalization makes the eigenfunctions orthonormal. We use spherical coordinates x=(sin⁡θcos⁡φ,sin⁡θsin⁡φ,cos⁡θ)∈S2x=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)\in\mathbb S^2x=(sinθcosφ,sinθsinφ,cosθ)∈S2 for (θ,φ)∈[0,π]×[0,2π](\theta,\varphi) \in [0,\pi] \times [0,2\pi](θ,φ)∈[0,π]×[0,2π].

For a fixed ℓ\ellℓ, the space Vℓ=span(φℓ,m)V_\ell = \text{span}( \varphi_{\ell,m} )Vℓ​=span(φℓ,m​) is an eigenspace of Δ\DeltaΔ, and is also invariant under rotation.

One can take φ1=N−1/21\varphi_1=N^{-1/2}\mathbb{1}φ1​=N−1/21, with 0=λ1⩾λ2⩾⋯⩾λN0=\lambda_1\geqslant\lambda_2\geqslant\cdots\geqslant\lambda_N0=λ1​⩾λ2​⩾⋯⩾λN​.
